posts.post_title: Who is regarded as the ‘Father of Immunology…
posts.post_content: Who is regarded as the ‘Father of Immunology’ for demonstrating vaccination using cowpox material?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Edward Jenner

Edward Jenner (1749-1823) is considered the Father of Immunology.

Correct Option Explanation

In 1798, Jenner inoculated an eight-year-old boy with cowpox blister fluid and protected him from severe smallpox, naming the technique vaccination.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Louis Pasteur developed vaccines for anthrax, rabies and fowl cholera decades later.
  • Robert Koch is known for germ theory and 1891 discovery of delayed type hypersensitivity.
  • Paul Ehrlich proposed the side chain theory of antibody formation in 1900.
Know More
  • Benjamin Jesty inoculated his wife with vaccinia in 1774, before Jenner.
  • Vacca is Latin for cow, the root of ‘vaccination’.
  • Chinese variolation predated Jenner by centuries.
  • Smallpox was globally eradicated using Jenner’s principle.

posts.post_title: Louis Pasteur established the Pasteur Instit…
posts.post_content: Louis Pasteur established the Pasteur Institute and first administered his rabies vaccine to which patient in 1885?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Joseph Meister

Joseph Meister, a boy bitten by a rabid wolf, received Pasteur’s first rabies vaccine in 1885.

Correct Option Explanation

Pasteur dried rabid rabbit spinal cord to attenuate the virus; the boy did not develop rabies, proving the vaccine's success.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Benjamin Jesty inoculated his wife with vaccinia virus in 1774, unrelated to rabies.
  • Edward Jenner pioneered smallpox vaccination, not rabies.
  • Robert Koch worked on tuberculosis and germ theory, not rabies vaccination.
Know More
  • First human rabies vaccine trial was on 6 July 1885.
  • This date is observed as Zoonosis Day.
  • Pasteur applied attenuation earlier to control anthrax in sheep (1881).
  • Pasteur Institute, Paris, became a hub for immunology research.

posts.post_title: Which scientist first described phagocytosis…
posts.post_content: Which scientist first described phagocytosis and the cellular theory of immunity after observing rose-thorn injury in starfish larvae?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Elie Metchnikoff

Elie Metchnikoff (1845-1916), a Russian zoologist, discovered phagocytosis in 1882 using starfish larvae.

Correct Option Explanation

He extended this to Daphnia and mammalian leukocytes, defining phagocytosis by microphages and macrophages as the main defense.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Jules Bordet discovered complement and bacteriolysis in 1894.
  • Karl Landsteiner identified the ABO blood group in 1901.
  • Paul Ehrlich proposed the side chain (selective) theory of antibody formation in 1900.
Know More
  • Metchnikoff's theory competed with the humoral theory of immunity.
  • Phagocytes include microphages (PMNs) and larger macrophages.
  • Metchnikoff shared views validated ~50 years later.
  • The two schools of thought (cellular vs humoral) developed simultaneously in the 1880s.

posts.post_title: In which year did Von Behring and Kitasato d…
posts.post_content: In which year did Von Behring and Kitasato demonstrate toxin-antitoxin neutralization, providing the first proof of humoral immunity?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1890

In 1890, Von Behring and Shibasaburo Kitasato demonstrated antitoxin neutralization for diphtheria and tetanus toxin.

Correct Option Explanation

Transfer of immune serum conferred antitoxin immunity to non-immune animals, the first direct evidence of humoral immunity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1885 is when Pasteur administered the first rabies vaccine to Joseph Meister.
  • 1901 is when Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood group and Bordet & Gengou devised the CFT.
  • 1917 is when Karl Landsteiner described the concept of the hapten.
Know More
  • Von Behring won the first Nobel Prize in Medicine (1901) for this discovery.
  • Complement was earlier termed alexin by Hans Buchner in 1889.
  • Fodor (1886) had already shown direct bactericidal action of immune serum on anthrax bacilli.
  • Bordet later isolated complement's role in bacteriolysis (1894).

posts.post_title: Who proposed the clonal selection theory of…
posts.post_content: Who proposed the clonal selection theory of antibody formation and later shared the Nobel Prize with Medawar in 1960?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Frank Macfarlane Burnet

Frank Macfarlane Burnet proposed the clonal selection theory in 1957.

Correct Option Explanation

Burnet and Medawar received the Nobel Prize in 1960 for the theory of acquired immunological tolerance and clonal selection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Niels Jerne proposed the network theory and won the Nobel Prize in 1984.
  • Paul Ehrlich proposed the earlier side chain theory in 1900.
  • Susumu Tonegawa won the Nobel Prize in 1987 for gene rearrangement in antibody diversity.
Know More
  • Clonal selection theory: each lymphocyte recognizes only one antigen.
  • Self-reactive clones eliminated in embryonic life are called forbidden clones.
  • It is considered the most widely accepted theory of antibody formation.
  • Burnet and Jerne together were credited for clonal selection theory work (1955-59).

posts.post_title: Which discovery is credited to George Kohler…
posts.post_content: Which discovery is credited to George Kohler and Cesar Milstein in 1975?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Monoclonal antibodies

George Kohler and Cesar Milstein discovered monoclonal antibodies in 1975 using hybridoma technology.

Correct Option Explanation

They fused antibody-producing spleen cells with myeloma cells, creating hybridomas that secrete a single antibody specificity indefinitely.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Complement fixation test was devised by Bordet and Gengou in 1901.
  • ABO blood group was discovered by Landsteiner in 1901.
  • Interferon was discovered by Isaacs and Lindenmann in 1957.
Know More
  • Kohler and Milstein received the Nobel Prize for hybridoma technology.
  • HAT medium selects for successfully fused hybridoma cells.
  • Monoclonal antibodies are widely used in CELISA kits for bluetongue diagnosis.
  • Myeloma lines like SP2/0 BALB/c are commonly used fusion partners.

posts.post_title: The discovery of the Bursa of Fabricius as a…
posts.post_content: The discovery of the Bursa of Fabricius as a primary lymphoid organ is attributed to which scientist, in 1955?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Glick

Glick discovered the role of the Bursa of Fabricius in B-cell development in 1955.

Correct Option Explanation

This bird-specific organ was later shown essential for antibody-producing B lymphocyte maturation, distinguishing B cells from T cells.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Jules Bordet is known for complement and bacteriolysis discoveries (1894).
  • Karl Landsteiner discovered ABO blood groups (1901) and Rh antigen (1940).
  • Robert Koch described delayed type hypersensitivity (1891), unrelated to the bursa.
Know More
  • ‘B’ in B-lymphocyte derives from Bursa of Fabricius.
  • Bursa reaches maximum size 3 weeks after hatching.
  • Bursal hormone influencing maturation is called bursin/bursopoietin.
  • Mammals lack a bursa; B cells mature in bone marrow or Peyer's patches instead.

posts.post_title: The Weil-Felix reaction, used to detect anti…
posts.post_content: The Weil-Felix reaction, used to detect antibody against Rickettsial organisms, is based on cross-reactivity with which bacterial antigen?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Proteus antigen

The Weil-Felix reaction uses cross-reacting Proteus strains (OX-19, OX-2, OX-K) as a heterophile antigen.

Correct Option Explanation

These Proteus antigens are agglutinated by antibodies raised against Rickettsia rickettsii and related organisms due to shared heterophile antigens.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Salmonella O antigen is a somatic lipopolysaccharide antigen unrelated to Rickettsial cross-reaction.
  • E. coli K antigen is a capsular polysaccharide antigen, not linked to Weil-Felix.
  • Brucella antigen is used in brucellosis-specific serology, not Rickettsial diagnosis.
Know More
  • Frossman antigens are another heterophile antigen group shared by bacteria and RBCs of horses, sheep, cats and mice.
  • Heterophile antigens explain antigenic sharing across unrelated species.
  • Weil-Felix uses an agglutination test format.
  • Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

posts.post_title: Which scientist first used the term ‘allergy…
posts.post_content: Which scientist first used the term ‘allergy’ in 1906?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Clemens Pirquet

Clemens Pirquet introduced the term ‘allergy’ in 1906.

Correct Option Explanation

He used it to describe an altered state of reactivity of the body following exposure to a foreign substance.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Karl Landsteiner described the hapten concept in 1917, not allergy terminology.
  • Nicholas Arthus described specific tissue destruction, the Arthus Phenomenon, in 1903.
  • Almoth Wright described opsonization in 1903, not allergy.
Know More
  • Von Pirquet also studied serum sickness in 1905.
  • The Gell and Coombs classification (1963) later formalized hypersensitivity types.
  • Charles Richet and Portier described anaphylaxis in 1902.
  • Allergy is now classified mainly as Type I hypersensitivity.

posts.post_title: Susumu Tonegawa won the Nobel Prize in 1987…
posts.post_content: Susumu Tonegawa won the Nobel Prize in 1987 for his work on which topic?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Gene rearrangement in antibody diversity

Susumu Tonegawa won the 1987 Nobel Prize for elucidating gene rearrangement underlying antibody diversity.

Correct Option Explanation

He showed that V, D and J gene segments recombine during B cell differentiation to generate highly diverse immunoglobulin variable regions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Complement discovery traces to Bordet and earlier workers (1890s), not Tonegawa.
  • Interferon was discovered by Isaacs and Lindenmann in 1957.
  • Monoclonal antibody production (hybridoma technology) was developed by Kohler and Milstein in 1975.
Know More
  • Immunoglobulin genes are made of V, D, J and C segments.
  • Heavy chain V region uses V, D and J segments; light chain uses only V and J.
  • This work explained the vast diversity (10^8+) of antibody specificities.
  • Tonegawa worked at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

posts.post_title: Which organ is the first primary lymphoid or…
posts.post_content: Which organ is the first primary lymphoid organ to develop in mammals?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thymus

The thymus is the first lymphoid organ to develop in mammals, located in the anterior mediastinum.

Correct Option Explanation

It differentiates immature thymocytes into immunocompetent T lymphocytes through positive and negative selection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bursa of Fabricius is exclusive to birds, not mammals.
  • Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ, developing later in fetal life.
  • Bone marrow is the site of B cell maturation in most mammals, not the first organ to develop.
Know More
  • Thymus develops from invaginations of the ectoderm.
  • About 90-95% of thymocytes die by apoptosis during selection.
  • Thymic hormones include thymopoietin, thymosin, thymulin.
  • The thymus atrophies after puberty but remnants persist.

posts.post_title: In which primary lymphoid organ do B cells m…
posts.post_content: In which primary lymphoid organ do B cells mature in birds?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bursa of Fabricius

In birds, B cells mature in the Bursa of Fabricius, a sac-like organ near the cloaca.

Correct Option Explanation

Bursal stem cells differentiate into B lymphocytes under hormonal influence of bursin/bursopoietin, appearing between 12-15 days of embryonic life.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Thymus is where T cells, not B cells, mature.
  • Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ involved in filtering blood-borne antigens.
  • Lymph node is also a secondary lymphoid organ, not a site of primary B cell maturation.
Know More
  • Mammalian equivalents of the bursa include Peyer's patches and bone marrow.
  • Bursa also traps antigen and produces some antibody, unlike a pure primary organ.
  • Bursal follicles have a cortex and medulla like the thymus.
  • 'B' lymphocyte nomenclature is derived from Bursa.

posts.post_title: Which of the following is an example of a se…
posts.post_content: Which of the following is an example of a secondary lymphoid organ?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Spleen

The spleen is a classic secondary lymphoid organ where blood-borne antigens are trapped and immune responses generated.

Correct Option Explanation

Unlike primary organs, the spleen persists through adult life and its lymphocyte maturation is antigen-dependent.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Thymus is a primary lymphoid organ for T cell maturation.
  • Bone marrow's embryonic hematopoietic role classifies it functionally with primary lymphoid organs for B cell generation.
  • Bursa of Fabricius is a primary lymphoid organ specific to birds.
Know More
  • Other secondary organs include lymph nodes, tonsils, MALT, GALT.
  • Spleen's white pulp contains lymphocytes; red pulp filters aged RBCs.
  • Splenic marginal zone separates red and white pulp.
  • Removal of secondary organs has minimal effect compared to primary organ removal.

posts.post_title: Which cells within lymph node germinal centr…
posts.post_content: Which cells within lymph node germinal centres trap antigen and present it to B cells?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Follicular dendritic cells

Follicular dendritic cells (FDCs) in germinal centres trap antigen and present it to B cells.

Correct Option Explanation

Germinal centres are sites of B cell somatic maturation, immunoglobulin class switching and memory cell formation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Kupffer cells are liver macrophages, unrelated to lymph node germinal centres.
  • Langerhans cells are dendritic cells found in the skin epidermis.
  • Reticular cells form the supporting meshwork of lymphoid tissue, not antigen presentation specialists.
Know More
  • Primary follicles contain mainly naive, mature B cells.
  • Secondary follicles develop on antigenic stimulation.
  • About 70% of paracortical T cells are CD4+ helper cells.
  • Naive T cells enter lymph nodes via high endothelial venules (HEVs).

posts.post_title: The largest lymph vessel that empties lymph…
posts.post_content: The largest lymph vessel that empties lymph into the anterior vena cava is the:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thoracic duct

The thoracic duct is the largest lymph vessel, collecting lymph from the lower body and intestine.

Correct Option Explanation

It empties lymph, largely carrying recirculating T cells, into the anterior vena cava, maintaining circulating lymphocyte numbers.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Afferent lymphatic vessels carry lymph into lymph nodes, not to the vena cava.
  • Efferent lymphatic vessels carry lymph out of individual nodes, joining larger vessels.
  • Splenic artery supplies blood to the spleen, unrelated to lymphatic drainage.
Know More
  • Cannulating the thoracic duct significantly drops circulating T cell numbers.
  • 90% of lymphocytes leaving a node enter via HEVs.
  • HEVs are absent in sheep lymph nodes.
  • In pigs, lymphocytes recirculate back through HEVs rather than lymphatics.

posts.post_title: Which cells predominate in the periarterial…
posts.post_content: Which cells predominate in the periarterial lymphoid sheath (PALS) of the splenic white pulp?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: T cells

T cells cuff the trabecular arterioles forming the periarterial lymphoid sheath (PALS) in splenic white pulp.

Correct Option Explanation

PALS constitutes the T cell zone, while B cell follicles with germinal centres lie within it, together forming the white pulp.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • B cells occupy the follicles within PALS, not the sheath itself.
  • Neutrophils are not a defining cell type of splenic white pulp architecture.
  • Eosinophils are not the predominant PALS cell type either.
Know More
  • Germinal centres in splenic follicles are also called Malpighian corpuscles.
  • Red pulp destroys aged RBCs and platelets, called hemocatharesis.
  • Marginal zone separates white and red pulp, containing both T and B cells.
  • Spleen filters blood-borne antigen; lymph nodes filter lymph-borne antigen.

posts.post_title: Neutrophils originate from which tissue and…
posts.post_content: Neutrophils originate from which tissue and typically circulate in blood for how long before entering tissues?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bone marrow; 10-12 hours

Neutrophils originate in bone marrow and circulate in blood for only 10-12 hours before entering tissues.

Correct Option Explanation

Their bone marrow development takes about two weeks, and total lifespan is only a few days, lacking the capacity to multiply.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Thymus; 3-4 months describes neither neutrophil origin nor macrophage life span correctly.
  • Spleen; several days misattributes neutrophil origin, though eosinophils mature partly in spleen.
  • Liver; 20 minutes is incorrect for neutrophils; this figure loosely resembles eosinophil blood half-life (~30 minutes).
Know More
  • Neutrophils are called polymorphonuclear (PMN) leucocytes.
  • They constitute 60-75% of leucocytes in carnivores, 20-30% in ruminants.
  • Primary granules contain defensins and myeloperoxidase.
  • Macrophages differentiate from circulating monocytes.

posts.post_title: Which enzyme in neutrophil primary granules…
posts.post_content: Which enzyme in neutrophil primary granules causes the ‘respiratory burst’ reaction with hydrogen peroxide?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Myeloperoxidase

Myeloperoxidase catalyzes the reaction between hydrogen peroxide and halide ions to form microbicidal hypohalides.

Correct Option Explanation

This reaction, called the respiratory burst, follows superoxide generation by NADPH-oxidase after phagocytes bind foreign particles.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Lysozyme destroys bacterial cell walls but is not the respiratory burst enzyme.
  • Collagenase is a secondary granule enzyme that degrades connective tissue.
  • Elastase is a neutral protease that degrades bacterial products, unrelated to the oxidative burst.
Know More
  • The respiratory burst is also called the hexose-monophosphate shunt pathway.
  • Macrophages also produce nitric oxide via inducible NOS.
  • Primary (azurophilic) granules also contain defensins.
  • Secondary granules contain lactoferrin, an iron-binding protein.

posts.post_title: Which cell type is described as being able t…
posts.post_content: Which cell type is described as being able to differentiate into Kupffer cells, microglia, and osteoclasts depending on tissue location?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Macrophages

Macrophages differentiate into tissue-specific forms such as Kupffer cells (liver), microglia (CNS), and osteoclasts (bone).

Correct Option Explanation

All arise from bone marrow monocytes that circulate before maturing into resident macrophages with varied morphology per habitat.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Neutrophils are terminally differentiated and do not diversify into these tissue-specific forms.
  • Eosinophils mature partly in the spleen but do not form Kupffer cells or microglia.
  • Mast cells are bone marrow-derived resident cells but distinct from the mononuclear phagocyte lineage.
Know More
  • Alveolar macrophages reside in lungs; mesangial cells in kidneys.
  • All mononuclear phagocytes together form the reticuloendothelial system.
  • Macrophages secrete over 100 bioactive molecules including IL-1.
  • Macrophage life span is about 3-4 months.

posts.post_title: Eosinophils primarily kill IgE-coated parasi…
posts.post_content: Eosinophils primarily kill IgE-coated parasites through which process?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Antibody dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)

Eosinophils kill IgE-coated helminths via antibody dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), using Fc receptors specific for IgE.

Correct Option Explanation

They release major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein that are toxic to parasites resistant to neutrophil/macrophage lysosomal enzymes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Direct phagocytosis is limited since helminths are too large for eosinophil engulfment.
  • Complement fixation is not the mechanism eosinophils use against parasites.
  • Opsonization by IgM is unrelated; eosinophils use IgE-Fc receptor recognition instead.
Know More
  • Eosinophil crystalloid granules contain major basic protein.
  • Eosinophils participate in Type I hypersensitivity reactions.
  • Tissue eosinophil numbers are about 500 times blood levels.
  • Eosinophil blood half-life is roughly 30 minutes.

posts.post_title: Mast cells and basophils both bear high-affi…
posts.post_content: Mast cells and basophils both bear high-affinity Fc receptors specific for which immunoglobulin class?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: IgE

Mast cells and basophils carry high-affinity Fc receptors specific for IgE, enabling sensitization for Type I hypersensitivity.

Correct Option Explanation

IgE binding cross-links on the cell surface upon antigen re-exposure, triggering degranulation and release of histamine and other mediators.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • IgG Fc receptors are found on macrophages and NK cells, not primarily mast cells/basophils.
  • IgA is mainly involved in mucosal immunity, not mast cell sensitization.
  • IgM is the first antibody in primary response and a strong complement activator, unrelated to mast cell Fc receptors.
Know More
  • Mast cell granules contain histamine, heparin, and TNF-alpha.
  • Basophils are the smallest granulocytes.
  • Mast cells are scattered beneath skin, lung alveoli and GI mucosa.
  • IgE-mediated reactions also aid defense against parasitic worms.

posts.post_title: Which cells constitute about 5-20% of mononu…
posts.post_content: Which cells constitute about 5-20% of mononuclear cells in blood and spleen and can kill target cells without prior activation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Natural killer (NK) cells

NK cells constitute 5-20% of blood and splenic mononuclear cells and kill targets without additional activation.

Correct Option Explanation

They are neither T nor B cells, use activating/inhibitory receptors, and kill via perforin and granzyme release causing apoptosis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • T helper cells require antigen presentation via MHC-II before activation, unlike NK cells.
  • B lymphocytes mediate humoral immunity through antibody secretion, not direct cytotoxic killing.
  • Neutrophils are phagocytes of the innate system, distinct from large granular lymphocyte NK cells.
Know More
  • NK cells are also called large granular lymphocytes.
  • Loss of class I MHC on infected cells triggers NK activation.
  • NK cells participate in ADCC like eosinophils.
  • IFN-gamma from NK cells enhances macrophage phagocytosis.

posts.post_title: Which membrane molecule is characteristicall…
posts.post_content: Which membrane molecule is characteristically expressed on cytotoxic T cells?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: CD8

CD8 is the surface molecule expressed on cytotoxic/suppressor T cells.

Correct Option Explanation

CD8+ T cells recognize antigen presented with MHC class I and destroy virus-infected or tumor cells.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • CD4 marks helper T cells, which recognize antigen with MHC class II.
  • CD19 is a B cell surface marker, not a T cell marker.
  • CD21 is a B cell complement receptor (CR2), unrelated to cytotoxic T cells.
Know More
  • CD3 complex associates with the T cell receptor on all T cells.
  • CD2 is the receptor for CD58 on T cells.
  • CD25 is the interleukin-2 receptor important for T cell growth.
  • Cytotoxic T cells cause transplant rejection along with tumor and virus-infected cell killing.

posts.post_title: Which subset of T helper cells secretes cyto…
posts.post_content: Which subset of T helper cells secretes cytokines that support humoral (antibody-mediated) immune responses?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Th2

Th2 cells secrete cytokines that help drive humoral immune responses.

Correct Option Explanation

Th2-derived cytokines promote B cell activation, antibody class switching and production, distinguishing them from cell-mediated Th1 responses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Th1 cells secrete cytokines that support cell-mediated immunity, not humoral responses.
  • Th17 cells are linked to inflammation in autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, not primarily humoral help.
  • Treg (regulatory T) cells maintain immune tolerance rather than promoting antibody responses.
Know More
  • Th1 cells help cell-mediated immunity via macrophage activation.
  • gamma/delta T cells form up to 60% of circulating T cells in young ruminants.
  • NK T cells recognize glycolipid antigens presented by CD1.
  • Memory T cells may be CD4+ or CD8+.

posts.post_title: Which of the following is a defining feature…
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a defining feature of B lymphocytes that distinguishes them from T lymphocytes?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Presence of surface immunoglobulin

B cells uniquely display surface immunoglobulin (IgM, IgD, IgG) as their antigen receptor.

Correct Option Explanation

T cells lack surface immunoglobulin and instead express T cell receptors; B cells mediate humoral, not cell-mediated, immunity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Maturation in thymus is a T cell feature; B cells mature in bursa, bone marrow or Peyer's patches.
  • Long circulating life span (months to years) describes T cells; B cell life span is typically shorter.
  • Response to PHA mitogen is characteristic of T cells; B cells respond to pokeweed mitogen and LPS.
Know More
  • B cells form EAC rosettes with sheep RBC coated in antibody and complement.
  • T cells form E (SRBC) rosettes via CD2.
  • B cells can take up unprocessed antigen; T cells need processed antigen.
  • Plasma cells derived from B cells can secrete ~300 immunoglobulin molecules/second.

posts.post_title: Which statement correctly differentiates inn…
posts.post_content: Which statement correctly differentiates innate immunity from adaptive immunity?

_aimcq_options.text: Innate immunity has memory; adaptive does not
Adaptive immunity has memory; innate does not
Both have equal diversity of receptors
Innate immunity develops only after repeated exposure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Adaptive immunity has memory; innate does not

Adaptive immunity exhibits memory, enabling faster, stronger responses on re-exposure; innate immunity lacks this.

Correct Option Explanation

Memory cells generated during adaptive responses persist and rapidly generate secondary responses, a feature absent in innate defenses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Innate immunity does not have memory; describing it as having memory reverses the correct pairing.
  • Diversity is not equal; adaptive immunity has vastly greater receptor diversity from somatic recombination.
  • Innate immunity is present from birth, not developed only after repeated exposure like adaptive immunity.
Know More
  • Innate immunity uses germ-line encoded, limited diversity receptors.
  • Cardinal features of adaptive immunity: specificity, diversity, memory, self/non-self recognition.
  • Innate immunity is phylogenetically older than adaptive immunity.
  • Both systems show non-reactivity to self under normal conditions.

posts.post_title: Which pathway of complement activation is tr…
posts.post_content: Which pathway of complement activation is triggered directly by antibody bound to antigen?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Classical pathway

The classical pathway of complement activation is triggered by antibody (IgG or IgM) bound to antigen.

Correct Option Explanation

C1 binds to the CH2 domain of IgG or CH3 domain of IgM, initiating a cascade through C4, C2 and onward to C3 convertase.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alternative pathway is activated by microbial surfaces independent of antibody.
  • Lectin pathway is activated by mannose-binding protein binding microbial sugars, not antibody.
  • Terminal pathway begins after C5 convertase formation from any of the three initiating pathways, not a separate trigger.
Know More
  • IgM, being pentameric, is more efficient than IgG at fixing complement.
  • C4b2a is the classical pathway C3 convertase.
  • C1 comprises C1q, C1r and C1s bound by calcium.
  • C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) normally prevents inappropriate C1 activation.

posts.post_title: In the alternative complement pathway, which…
posts.post_content: In the alternative complement pathway, which plasma protein forms the C3 convertase together with C3b?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Factor B (as Bb)

In the alternative pathway, C3b binds Factor B, which is cleaved by Factor D to form Bb, giving the C3bBb convertase.

Correct Option Explanation

Properdin stabilizes this complex, increasing its half-life from 5 to about 30 minutes, enhancing complement amplification on microbial surfaces.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • C1q is part of the classical pathway's recognition complex, not the alternative pathway convertase.
  • C4b combines with C2a in the classical pathway convertase (C4b2a), not the alternative pathway.
  • Mannose-binding lectin initiates the lectin pathway, structurally similar to C1q but functionally distinct.
Know More
  • Factor D is a plasma serine protease that cleaves Factor B.
  • Properdin (Factor P) stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase.
  • C3bBb3b acts as the alternative pathway C5 convertase.
  • Mammalian cell surfaces are protected by sialylation, resisting alternative pathway activation.

posts.post_title: The membrane attack complex (MAC) responsibl…
posts.post_content: The membrane attack complex (MAC) responsible for complement-mediated cell lysis is composed of which terminal components?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: C5b678(9)n

The membrane attack complex is a transmembrane pore formed by C5b678(9)n, with multiple C9 molecules.

Correct Option Explanation

C5b initiates binding of C6, C7 and C8, then 12-18 C9 molecules polymerize to form the doughnut-shaped pore causing osmotic lysis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • C1q, C1r, C1s form the initiating C1 complex of the classical pathway, not the MAC.
  • C3a, C4a, C5a are anaphylatoxins that trigger mast cell degranulation, distinct from the pore-forming MAC.
  • C4b2a3b is the classical pathway C5 convertase, which generates C5b but is not the MAC itself.
Know More
  • MAC causes osmotic lysis via a transmembrane channel.
  • C5a is also a potent chemotactic and anaphylatoxin peptide.
  • Anaphylatoxins C3a, C4a, C5a trigger histamine release from mast cells.
  • MAC formation is the terminal, common step of all three complement pathways.

posts.post_title: Which serum, due to containing all lytic com…
posts.post_content: Which serum, due to containing all lytic complement factors in correct proportion, is preferred as the best source of complement for laboratory tests?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Guinea pig serum

Guinea pig serum contains all lytic complement factors in correct proportion, making it the preferred complement source.

Correct Option Explanation

Fresh, preferably pooled guinea pig serum is used in the complement fixation test since it reliably provides functional complement activity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Horse serum complement is described as incomplete and poorly lytic.
  • Mouse serum complement is also noted as incomplete and poorly lytic.
  • Human serum is not specifically cited as the standard laboratory complement source in this context.
Know More
  • Hemolysis or tissue damage during collection releases anticomplementary factors.
  • Complement constitutes about 10% of serum globular protein fraction.
  • At least 19 heat-labile complement proteins exist, inactivated at 56°C for 30 min.
  • Complement fixation test uses sheep RBC-antibody as the indicator system.

posts.post_title: Which factor acts as a cofactor for Factor I…
posts.post_content: Which factor acts as a cofactor for Factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b, thereby regulating the complement system?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Factor H

Factor H binds C3b, displaces Bb, and acts as a cofactor for Factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b.

Correct Option Explanation

This regulatory action limits alternative pathway amplification and prevents complement damage to host tissues.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • C4 binding protein is a cofactor for Factor I cleavage of C4b, not C3b, in the classical pathway.
  • C1-INH dissociates C1r and C1s from C1q, controlling classical pathway assembly, not C3b cleavage.
  • Decay accelerating factor (DAF) displaces C2b from C4b and Bb from C3b rather than acting as a Factor I cofactor.
Know More
  • Membrane cofactor protein (MCP) also assists Factor I cleavage of C3b and C4b.
  • Vitronectin/clusterin block C9 binding, preventing MAC formation.
  • Factor I is itself a serine protease.
  • These regulators protect normal host cells from complement attack.

posts.post_title: Which of the following is a component or fra…
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a component or fragment of complement, rather than a regulatory protein?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: C3a

C3a is a peptide fragment generated by cleavage of C3, acting as an anaphylatoxin.

Correct Option Explanation

C3a, along with C4a and C5a, triggers mast cell degranulation and histamine release, unlike the listed regulatory proteins.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Factor H is a regulatory protein that displaces Bb and assists Factor I cleavage of C3b.
  • DAF (decay accelerating factor) regulates complement by displacing convertase components.
  • C1-INH is a regulatory serine protease inhibitor controlling classical pathway activation.
Know More
  • C3a, C4a and C5a are collectively called anaphylatoxins.
  • C5a is also strongly chemotactic for neutrophils.
  • Complement fragments are denoted with lowercase letters (e.g., C3a, C3b).
  • Enzymatically active complexes are denoted with a bar over the symbol.

posts.post_title: The ability of a molecule to induce a humora…
posts.post_content: The ability of a molecule to induce a humoral and/or cell mediated immune response is termed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Immunogenicity

Immunogenicity is the ability of a substance to induce a humoral and/or cell mediated immune response.

Correct Option Explanation

All immunogenic molecules are antigenic, but not all antigenic molecules are immunogenic; the reverse relationship does not hold.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Antigenicity is only the ability to be recognized by an antibody or lymphocyte, not necessarily to induce a response.
  • Hapten activity refers to small molecules needing a carrier to become immunogenic, not the general property being defined.
  • Avidity describes the overall strength of multivalent antigen-antibody binding, unrelated to this definition.
Know More
  • Haptens have antigenicity but not immunogenicity alone.
  • Molecular size, complexity, shape, and foreignness all affect immunogenicity.
  • Larger molecular weight generally improves antigenicity, with exceptions like glucagon.
  • Genotype of the recipient (MHC genes) influences immune responsiveness.

posts.post_title: Which factor makes penicillin and aspirin po…
posts.post_content: Which factor makes penicillin and aspirin poor antigens on their own?

_aimcq_options.text: Their molecular weight is less than 1000 daltons
They are too large to be phagocytosed
They are highly stable and rigid
They are foreign to all species

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Their molecular weight is less than 1000 daltons

Penicillin and aspirin have molecular weight below 1000 daltons, making them poor antigens alone.

Correct Option Explanation

Larger molecular weight generally correlates with better antigenicity; such small molecules act as haptens requiring a carrier protein.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Being too large is the opposite issue; small size, not large size, limits their antigenicity here.
  • Stability and rigidity actually favor antigenicity (e.g., gelatin is unstable and a poor antigen); this is not why penicillin fails alone.
  • Being foreign is necessary but not sufficient; foreignness alone doesn't overcome the low molecular weight limitation.
Know More
  • Ovalbumin (40,000 Da) is a good antigen due to larger size.
  • Glucagon (2600 Da) is an exception, being immunogenic despite small size.
  • Haptens like penicillin need coupling to a carrier protein to elicit antibodies.
  • Penicillin allergy arises when the penicilloyl group binds host proteins.

posts.post_title: Haptens are best described as:
posts.post_content: Haptens are best described as:

_aimcq_options.text: Small molecules that are antigenic but not immunogenic alone
Antigens found only on RBC surfaces

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Small molecules that are antigenic but not immunogenic alone

Haptens are small, usually non-protein molecules that are antigenic (react with antibody) but not immunogenic alone.

Correct Option Explanation

They require conjugation to a carrier protein to induce antibody formation, hence also called partial antigens.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Large carbohydrate antigens are generally complete antigens, not haptens by definition.
  • RBC-surface-only antigens describes blood group antigens, not the general hapten concept.
  • Complete antigens requiring no carrier is the opposite of a hapten's defining feature.
Know More
  • The term 'hapten' derives from Greek 'haptein' meaning to fasten.
  • Examples include Penicillin and Dinitrophenyl (DNP).
  • Complex haptens are polyvalent and can precipitate; simple haptens are univalent and cannot.
  • Conjugated antigen formed from hapten and carrier is called an azoprotein.

posts.post_title: Epitopes recognized by B cells typically con…
posts.post_content: Epitopes recognized by B cells typically contain how many amino acids?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 10-15

B-cell epitopes typically comprise 10-15 amino acids, the smallest unit determining antigenic specificity.

Correct Option Explanation

Epitopes present specific spatial chemical groupings recognized by the antibody's paratope on its hypervariable region.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 6-10 amino acids is characteristic of T-cell epitopes, not B-cell epitopes.
  • 20-25 amino acids exceeds the typical epitope size described for either B or T cell recognition.
  • 30-40 amino acids is far larger than any epitope size mentioned for antigen recognition.
Know More
  • The antibody combining region is called the paratope or idiotope.
  • The T cell recognition site is termed the agretope.
  • Epitopes are also known as antigenic determinants.
  • T-cell epitopes are 6-10 amino acids long.

posts.post_title: Frossman antigens are an example of which ty…
posts.post_content: Frossman antigens are an example of which type of antigen?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Heterophile antigen

Frossman antigens are heterophile antigens shared between certain bacteria and red blood cells of several animal species.

Correct Option Explanation

They occur in bacterial cell walls (Streptococcus, Shigella, Salmonella, Clostridium) and RBCs of horses, sheep, cats and mice, causing antigenic cross-reaction.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alloantigens are present in some individuals of a species and antigenic to others of the same species, unlike shared cross-species Frossman antigens.
  • Autoantigens arise from an individual's own tissue, unrelated to bacterial-RBC antigen sharing.
  • Syngenic antigens are shared among genetically identical individuals like monozygotic twins, not cross-species bacteria/RBC sharing.
Know More
  • Animals with Frossman antigens don't form antibodies against them as they're 'self'.
  • Weil-Felix reaction uses another heterophile antigen (Proteus).
  • Heterophile antigens illustrate antigenic sharing across species.
  • Alloantibodies target alloantigens such as blood group antigens.

posts.post_title: Which type of antigen does NOT require proce…
posts.post_content: Which type of antigen does NOT require processing by antigen presenting cells to activate T cells, acting instead by directly cross-linking MHC and TCR?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Superantigen

Superantigens activate T cells without requiring processing by antigen presenting cells.

Correct Option Explanation

They directly bind outside the normal peptide groove, cross-linking MHC class II and T cell receptors non-specifically, causing massive T cell activation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • T-dependent antigens like RBC and serum proteins require T cell help and are metabolized/processed normally.
  • T-independent antigens (e.g., LPS, flagellin) do not require T cell help but still don't describe the superantigen mechanism.
  • Autoantigens are self-tissue components inducing autoimmunity, unrelated to the superantigen mechanism.
Know More
  • Streptococcal A antigen is a classic bacterial superantigen example.
  • T-independent antigens produce no memory or class switching.
  • T-dependent antigens require T cell help and induce memory/class switching.
  • Superantigens can cause toxic-shock-like massive cytokine release.

posts.post_title: Which bacterial antigen is composed of a lip…
posts.post_content: Which bacterial antigen is composed of a lipopolysaccharide-protein complex and is highly variable between strains?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Somatic (O) antigen

The somatic (O) antigen of gram-negative bacteria is a lipopolysaccharide-protein complex, highly variable due to variable oligosaccharide chains.

Correct Option Explanation

Because O antigens vary widely, immunity to one O antigen does not confer protection against bacteria bearing different O antigens.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Flagellar (H) antigen is a protein (flagellin) component of bacterial flagella, structurally distinct from LPS-based O antigen.
  • Capsular (K) antigen is typically polysaccharide (sometimes polypeptide), forming the bacterial capsule rather than LPS.
  • Fimbrial (F) antigen is present on bacterial pili/fimbriae, unrelated to the somatic LPS complex.
Know More
  • A common core polysaccharide underlying O antigens has vaccine potential.
  • Motile bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli possess H (flagellar) antigens.
  • Capsular antigen examples include K antigen of E. coli and poly-D-glutamic acid of B. anthracis.
  • Spore antigens occur in Bacillus and Clostridium species.

posts.post_title: MHC class I molecules are expressed on the s…
posts.post_content: MHC class I molecules are expressed on the surface of:

_aimcq_options.text: Nucleated cells (except erythrocytes in most species)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Nucleated cells (except erythrocytes in most species)

MHC class I molecules are expressed on virtually all nucleated cells, generally excluding erythrocytes in most species.

Correct Option Explanation

This broad distribution allows class I to present endogenous (e.g., viral) peptides to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells for immune surveillance.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Only B lymphocytes understates class I distribution; class I is on nearly all nucleated cells, while class II is mainly on APCs like B cells.
  • Only macrophages and dendritic cells describes class II expression, not class I.
  • Only serum proteins describes class III molecules like complement components, not class I.
Know More
  • MHC class II is expressed mainly on B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells.
  • MHC class III includes complement system proteins.
  • Human MHC is called HLA; bovine is BOLA; equine is ELA.
  • MHC restriction requires T cells to recognize antigen with self MHC.

posts.post_title: The endogenous antigen processing pathway, p…
posts.post_content: The endogenous antigen processing pathway, presenting peptides via MHC class I to cytotoxic T cells, relies on which transporter proteins?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: TAP1 and TAP2

Endogenous antigens are processed by immunoproteasomes, and peptides are transported by TAP1 and TAP2 to the endoplasmic reticulum for MHC class I loading.

Correct Option Explanation

This loaded MHC class I-peptide complex then reaches the cell surface, where cytotoxic T cells recognize it and lyse infected cells.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Igα and Igβ are signal-transducing molecules associated with the B cell receptor, unrelated to MHC I loading.
  • CD3 and CD28 are T cell surface molecules involved in TCR signaling and costimulation, not antigen transport.
  • C3b and C4b are complement fragments, unrelated to intracellular peptide transport for MHC.
Know More
  • Exogenous antigen processing uses MHC class II via phagosome-endosome fusion.
  • CD4+ T cells recognize peptide with MHC class II.
  • Non-peptide antigens like glycolipids are presented via CD1 molecules.
  • Immunoproteasomes degrade cytosolic proteins for class I loading.

posts.post_title: In the ABO blood group system, which group i…
posts.post_content: In the ABO blood group system, which group is used as the universal blood donor because its RBCs lack A and B antigens?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Group O

Group O RBCs lack both A and B antigens, so they are not agglutinated by serum from any other blood group, making O the universal donor.

Correct Option Explanation

However, group O serum contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, meaning O individuals can only receive blood from other O donors.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Group A carries the A antigen and would react with anti-A antibodies present in B or O sera.
  • Group B carries the B antigen and would react with anti-B antibodies in A or O sera.
  • Group AB lacks antibodies against A or B, making it the universal acceptor, not donor.
Know More
  • AB group is the universal acceptor, lacking anti-A/anti-B antibodies.
  • Isoantibodies appear in serum by about six months of age.
  • Group A subdivides into A1 (~80%) and A2 (~20%).
  • Blood group antigens are typically glycoproteins or glycolipids.

posts.post_title: Which antigen in the Rh blood group system i…
posts.post_content: Which antigen in the Rh blood group system is considered the most powerful and responsible for the majority of Rh incompatibility reactions?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: D (Rho) antigen

The D (Rho) antigen is the most powerful Rh antigen and responsible for most Rh incompatibility reactions.

Correct Option Explanation

Rh-negative individuals lack the D antigen; exposure to Rh-positive (D+) blood, as in erythroblastosis fetalis, triggers strong antibody responses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • C antigen is a weaker, cross-reactive Rh antigen, not the main cause of incompatibility.
  • E antigen is likewise a weaker, cross-reactive Rh system component compared to D.
  • M antigen belongs to the MN blood group system, unrelated to Rh incompatibility.
Know More
  • Rh antigens are determined by three linked allelomorphic gene pairs (Cc, Dd, Ee).
  • Landsteiner and Wiener identified the Rh factor in 1940 using rhesus monkey antiserum.
  • Erythroblastosis fetalis results from maternal IgG anti-Rh crossing the placenta.
  • Levine and Stetson first described related antibodies in 1939.

posts.post_title: Tiselius and Kabat, using electrophoresis of…
posts.post_content: Tiselius and Kabat, using electrophoresis of immune serum in 1938, found most immunoglobulins in which serum protein fraction?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Gamma (γ) globulin fraction

Tiselius and Kabat (1938) found most immunoglobulins concentrated in the gamma (γ) globulin fraction of serum.

Correct Option Explanation

Electrophoresis separated serum proteins into albumin, alpha, beta and gamma fractions, with antibody activity predominantly in gamma.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Albumin fraction does not contain immunoglobulins; it is the most abundant non-antibody serum protein.
  • Alpha (α) globulin fraction contains other transport proteins, not the bulk of immunoglobulins.
  • Beta (β) globulin fraction only is incomplete; while IgA and IgM show some beta mobility, most Ig is in the gamma fraction.
Know More
  • This work confirmed antibodies as gamma globulins (1939, Tiselius and Kabat).
  • Immunoglobulins make up about 20% of plasma proteins.
  • Antibody sediments mainly at 7S or 19S (Svedberg units).
  • IgG has the lowest electrophoretic mobility among immunoglobulins.

posts.post_title: An immunoglobulin monomer is composed of how…
posts.post_content: An immunoglobulin monomer is composed of how many peptide chains, forming its characteristic Y shape?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2 heavy chains and 2 light chains

An immunoglobulin monomer consists of 2 identical heavy chains and 2 identical light chains linked by disulphide bonds.

Correct Option Explanation

This arrangement produces the characteristic Y shape, with Fab arms for antigen binding and an Fc tail for effector functions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 4 heavy chains only omits the essential light chains required for the Y structure.
  • 1 heavy and 1 light chain would form only half the structure, insufficient for the bivalent Y shape.
  • 3 heavy and 1 light chain does not match the symmetric two-heavy, two-light chain arrangement.
Know More
  • Heavy chains weigh 50-60 KDa; light chains weigh 25 KDa.
  • Light chains are either kappa or lambda, never both in one molecule.
  • Two heavy chains are joined by disulphide bonds at the hinge.
  • The Fc region attaches to cell membranes or mediates effector functions.

posts.post_title: Which immunoglobulin heavy chain type corres…
posts.post_content: Which immunoglobulin heavy chain type corresponds to IgM?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mu (μ)

IgM has heavy chains of the mu (μ) type, giving the class its distinguishing identity.

Correct Option Explanation

Mu heavy chains contain an extra CH4 domain and lack a hinge region, contributing to IgM's unique pentameric structure.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Gamma (γ) heavy chains define IgG, not IgM.
  • Alpha (α) heavy chains define IgA, not IgM.
  • Epsilon (ε) heavy chains define IgE, not IgM.
Know More
  • Delta (δ) heavy chains correspond to IgD.
  • Mu and epsilon heavy chains have four constant domains, unlike gamma/alpha/delta with three plus a hinge.
  • IgM pentamers are linked by a J chain.
  • IgM lacks a hinge region.

posts.post_title: Which immunoglobulin is the first antibody p…
posts.post_content: Which immunoglobulin is the first antibody produced during the primary immune response?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: IgM

IgM is the first antibody produced in the primary immune response to an antigen.

Correct Option Explanation

It has high avidity due to its pentameric structure and is highly efficient at complement fixation and agglutination compared to IgG.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • IgG appears later than IgM but persists longer, dominating secondary immune responses.
  • IgA is mainly associated with mucosal immunity, not primary systemic response timing.
  • IgE is associated with allergic and antiparasitic responses, not primary response kinetics.
Know More
  • IgM is 500-1000 times more effective than IgG in opsonization.
  • A single IgM molecule can cause immune hemolysis; 1000 IgG molecules are needed for the same effect.
  • 2-mercaptoethanol disrupts IgM pentamers into monomers.
  • IgM sedimentation coefficient is 19S with a J chain linking five monomers.

posts.post_title: Which immunoglobulin class is the only one c…
posts.post_content: Which immunoglobulin class is the only one capable of crossing the placental barrier in most species?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: IgG

IgG is the only immunoglobulin class able to cross the placental barrier, providing passive immunity to the fetus.

Correct Option Explanation

Its smaller size (7S, 160 KDa) allows it to escape blood vessels and enter extravascular tissues and, in many species, the placenta.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • IgM is too large (19S pentamer) to cross the placenta.
  • IgA primarily protects mucosal surfaces and is transferred via colostrum, not the placenta.
  • IgE is not transferred across the placenta; it functions in allergic and antiparasitic responses.
Know More
  • IgG constitutes about 80% of total immunoglobulin and 20% of plasma proteins.
  • IgG subclasses vary by species: cattle have IgG1, IgG2 and IgG3.
  • IgG has the lowest carbohydrate content (about 3%) among immunoglobulins.
  • CH3 domain of IgG Fc binds macrophages for biological activity.

posts.post_title: Secretory IgA (SIgA) found on mucosal surfac…
posts.post_content: Secretory IgA (SIgA) found on mucosal surfaces is stabilized against proteolysis by which component?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Secretory component (Sc)

The secretory component (Sc), a glycoprotein made by mucosal epithelial cells, protects secretory IgA from gastrointestinal proteolysis.

Correct Option Explanation

SIgA is a dimer of two 7S IgA monomers joined by a J chain and wrapped with the Sc, forming an 11S, 360 KDa complex.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • J chain alone links the two IgA monomers together but does not itself confer proteolytic resistance; Sc provides that protection.
  • C1q is part of the complement classical pathway, unrelated to IgA stabilization.
  • Kappa light chain is a structural component of the antibody but does not protect against proteolysis.
Know More
  • Secretory component synthesis is independent of IgA production itself.
  • IgA subclasses IgA1 and IgA2 exist; IgA2 lacks heavy-light chain disulphide bonds.
  • IgA activates the alternative complement pathway but not the classical pathway.
  • Fecal IgA antibodies are called copro-antibodies.

posts.post_title: Which immunoglobulin class mediates Type I (…
posts.post_content: Which immunoglobulin class mediates Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reactions by binding to mast cells and basophils?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: IgE

IgE mediates Type I hypersensitivity by binding via its Fc region to mast cells and basophils, sensitizing them for allergen response.

Correct Option Explanation

Cross-linking of IgE upon antigen exposure triggers mast cell degranulation, releasing histamine and other mediators causing immediate hypersensitivity symptoms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • IgG mediates Type II and III hypersensitivity mechanisms, not the immediate IgE-mediated type.
  • IgA functions mainly in mucosal defense, not mast cell sensitization.
  • IgD has an unclear function, mainly associated with B cell development, not hypersensitivity.
Know More
  • IgE has the lowest serum concentration and shortest half-life among immunoglobulins.
  • IgE does not fix complement.
  • IgE provides some protection against parasitic worms.
  • IgE binds mast cells through its CH3 and CH4 domains.

posts.post_title: Predominant serum immunoglobulin in birds, s…
posts.post_content: Predominant serum immunoglobulin in birds, structurally similar to mammalian IgG, is called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: IgY

The predominant avian serum immunoglobulin, functionally analogous to mammalian IgG, is called IgY.

Correct Option Explanation

Chickens possess the full-sized 180 KDa isoform; ducks and geese also have a truncated 120 KDa isoform of IgY.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • IgW is not an avian immunoglobulin class described in this context.
  • IgX is not the term used for the avian IgG-analogous antibody.
  • IgZ is not the correct designation; it is unrelated to avian humoral immunity nomenclature here.
Know More
  • IgY heavy chain is designated epsilon in this text's nomenclature.
  • Monomeric IgM is detectable in amniotic fluid and day-old chicks.
  • Avian IgA is present in secretions and forms polymers.
  • An avian homolog of IgD has also been identified.

posts.post_title: Bence Jones proteins, found in the urine of…
posts.post_content: Bence Jones proteins, found in the urine of multiple myeloma patients, consist of excess:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Immunoglobulin light chains

Bence Jones proteins are excess free immunoglobulin light chains excreted in the urine of myeloma patients.

Correct Option Explanation

They precipitate when urine is warmed and characteristically re-dissolve upon further heating, a classic diagnostic feature.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Complement C3 fragments are unrelated to the plasma cell dyscrasia underlying Bence Jones proteinuria.
  • Heavy chain J segments are gene segments encoding heavy chain variable regions, not the excreted urinary protein.
  • MHC class I molecules are cell surface antigen-presenting molecules, unrelated to Bence Jones proteins.
Know More
  • Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy causing abnormal immunoglobulin production.
  • Allotypes are inherited structural variants of immunoglobulins between individuals.
  • Idiotypes arise from variable domain amino acid sequence differences.
  • Bence Jones proteins are a classic abnormal immunoglobulin finding.

posts.post_title: What structural feature allows the Fab arms…
posts.post_content: What structural feature allows the Fab arms of an antibody to swing around the central molecule?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The hinge region

The hinge region, located between CH1 and CH2 domains, allows Fab arms to swing, enabling flexible antigen binding.

Correct Option Explanation

It is proline-rich and hydrophilic, roughly 12 amino acids long, and is unique in sequence for each immunoglobulin class and subclass.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The J chain links IgM or IgA monomers together, not the flexibility of Fab arms within a monomer.
  • The secretory component protects secretory IgA from degradation, unrelated to Fab flexibility.
  • The CH4 domain is an additional constant domain present in mu and epsilon chains, not the flexible hinge.
Know More
  • Mu and epsilon heavy chains lack a hinge region.
  • Papain digestion at the hinge yields two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment.
  • Pepsin digestion yields an F(ab')2 fragment plus digested Fc fragments.
  • IgD's hinge lacks cysteine residues, so no interchain disulfide links form there.

posts.post_title: The light chain type predominating in cattle…
posts.post_content: The light chain type predominating in cattle and horse immunoglobulins (about 95%) is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lambda (λ)

In cattle and horses, about 95% of light chains are lambda (λ) type, contrasting with rodents which favor kappa.

Correct Option Explanation

Light chain type distribution varies markedly by species: rats and mice have over 95% kappa, while monkeys show about 50% of each.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Kappa (κ) predominates in rodents and about 60% in humans, not in cattle/horses.
  • Mu (μ) is a heavy chain type (defining IgM), not a light chain type at all.
  • Gamma (γ) is likewise a heavy chain type (defining IgG), not a light chain.
Know More
  • Light chains are 25 KDa and have two domains of 110 amino acids each.
  • Kappa and lambda names derive from their original describers, Koragold and Lapori.
  • Each immunoglobulin has either kappa or lambda light chains, never both.
  • Humans show about 60% kappa light chains.

posts.post_title: Which immunoglobulin subclass in cattle IgG…
posts.post_content: Which immunoglobulin subclass in cattle IgG shows fewer interchain disulfide bonds at the hinge compared to IgG2 and IgG3?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: IgG1

IgG1 has fewer interchain disulphide bonds at the hinge region compared to IgG2, IgG3 and IgG4.

Correct Option Explanation

The number of disulphide linkages between heavy chains at the hinge increases in the order IgG1 < IgG4 < IgG2 < IgG3.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • IgG2 has more interchain disulphide bonds at the hinge than IgG1.
  • IgG3 has the most interchain disulphide bonds among the listed subclasses in this ordering.
  • IgG4 also has more hinge disulphide bonds than IgG1, though fewer than IgG2 and IgG3.
Know More
  • Cattle IgG has three recognized subclasses: IgG1, IgG2 and IgG3.
  • Horses have six IgG subclasses: IgG1 through IgG6.
  • Dogs and cats have four IgG subclasses similar to humans.
  • Human IgG subclasses in decreasing serum concentration are IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, IgG4.

posts.post_title: Paul Ehrlich's side chain theory of antibody…
posts.post_content: Paul Ehrlich's side chain theory of antibody formation was abandoned after Landsteiner demonstrated:

_aimcq_options.text: Antibodies are produced against synthetic chemicals as well as natural antigens
T cells alone are responsible for antibody production

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Antibodies are produced against synthetic chemicals as well as natural antigens

Ehrlich's theory was abandoned once Landsteiner showed antibodies form against synthetic chemicals, not just natural antigens.

Correct Option Explanation

This contradicted the side chain theory's assumption of a fixed, pre-existing repertoire of natural receptors for known antigens only.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Antibodies never bind synthetic chemicals' is the opposite of what Landsteiner actually demonstrated.
  • 'Antigens must be proteins only' misstates the finding; Landsteiner's work involved diverse synthetic haptens, not a protein-only rule.
  • 'T cells alone are responsible' is unrelated; this theory concerns antibody-forming (B) cells, and T cells were not the focus of Ehrlich's or Landsteiner's work here.
Know More
  • Ehrlich proposed the side chain theory in 1900.
  • The theory proposed cell surface receptors act as antibody 'side chains'.
  • Excess receptors were postulated to be released as circulating antibodies.
  • Landsteiner's hapten-carrier work reshaped antigen specificity concepts.

posts.post_title: The clonal selection theory assumes that eac…
posts.post_content: The clonal selection theory assumes that each immunocompetent B lymphocyte:

_aimcq_options.text: Can recognize only one antigen and synthesize one type of immunoglobulin
Requires antigen to acquire genetic information for antibody synthesis

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Can recognize only one antigen and synthesize one type of immunoglobulin

Clonal selection theory holds that each B lymphocyte recognizes only one antigen and produces one immunoglobulin specificity.

Correct Option Explanation

Antigen binding stimulates proliferation of that specific clone into memory cells and antibody-secreting plasma cells, explaining specificity and memory.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Recognize all antigens simultaneously' contradicts the theory's premise of restricted, clone-specific recognition.
  • 'Loses receptors after birth' is not part of the theory; receptors persist and are used for antigen recognition throughout the cell's life.
  • 'Requires antigen for genetic information' describes instructive theories, which clonal selection (a selective theory) explicitly rejects.
Know More
  • Burnet proposed clonal selection theory in 1957.
  • Self-reactive clones eliminated during development are called forbidden clones.
  • Their persistence can cause autoimmune disease.
  • Medawar and Burnet shared the 1960 Nobel Prize for related tolerance work.

posts.post_title: According to the network theory proposed by…
posts.post_content: According to the network theory proposed by Jerne, anti-idiotype antibodies are produced against:

_aimcq_options.text: The idiotype (variable region) of another antibody

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The idiotype (variable region) of another antibody

Network theory proposes that the unique variable-region sequence (idiotype) of an antibody itself acts as an antigen, generating anti-idiotype antibodies.

Correct Option Explanation

This creates a regulatory idiotype network that helps control the magnitude and duration of antibody responses.

Incorrect Options Analysis

posts.post_title: Somatic mutation theory of antibody diversit…
posts.post_content: Somatic mutation theory of antibody diversity proposes that diversity mainly arises through:

Complete absence of germline V genes

posts.post_title: Isotype switching allows a B cell to change…
posts.post_content: Isotype switching allows a B cell to change antibody class (e.g., from IgM to IgG) while retaining:

Correct Answer: The same variable region/antigen specificity

posts.post_title: In hybridoma technology, myeloma cells used…
posts.post_content: In hybridoma technology, myeloma cells used for fusion are typically selected because they:

_aimcq_options.text: Do not secrete their own immunoglobulin
Secrete very high levels of immunoglobulin
Naturally produce monoclonal antibody against any antigen

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Do not secrete their own immunoglobulin

Myeloma cells used in hybridoma production are chosen because they do not secrete their own immunoglobulin, avoiding interference with the desired monoclonal antibody.

  • 'Secrete very high levels of immunoglobulin' is the opposite of the desirable trait, as this would contaminate the specific monoclonal antibody.

  • 'Naturally produce monoclonal antibody against any antigen' misunderstands the process; specificity comes from the fused spleen cell, not the myeloma partner.
Know More
  • HAT medium contains hypoxanthine, aminopterin and thymidine.

posts.post_title: Monoclonal antibody-based CELISA kits are wi…
posts.post_content: Monoclonal antibody-based CELISA kits are widely used for antibody detection against which disease in sheep?

Bluetongue disease antibody detection in sheep widely uses monoclonal antibody-based CELISA kits.

posts.post_title: Radio immunoassay (RIA) was first developed…
posts.post_content: Radio immunoassay (RIA) was first developed in the 1960s by which two endocrinologists to measure insulin-anti insulin complexes?

posts.post_title: Which fluorescent dye is most commonly used…
posts.post_content: Which fluorescent dye is most commonly used to label antibodies in immunofluorescence assays, emitting green fluorescence under UV light?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: FITC (fluorescein isothiocyanate)

FITC is the most commonly used fluorescent dye, emitting apple-green fluorescence around 525 nm under UV light.

FITC can be conjugated to antibodies without impairing their specific reactivity, making it ideal for direct and indirect FAT.

  • DAB (diaminobenzidine) is a chromogenic substrate forming an insoluble brown product used in IPT and dot ELISA, not a fluorescent dye.

posts.post_title: In the indirect fluorescent antibody test (I…
posts.post_content: In the indirect fluorescent antibody test (Indirect FAT) for detecting serum antibody, what is added after the test serum to visualize the reaction?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

In indirect FAT for antibody detection, FITC-labeled antiglobulin is added after test serum to visualize bound specific antibody.

Fluorescence under UV light after washing away unbound reagents indicates the test serum contained specific antibody to the antigen.

  • Radioactive iodine labeling belongs to RIA, a distinct primary binding technique, not FAT.

Know More

posts.post_title: In a sandwich ELISA for antigen detection, t…
posts.post_content: In a sandwich ELISA for antigen detection, the antibody first immobilized on the microtitre plate is called the:

The antibody immobilized on the plate to bind antigen from the sample is called the capture antibody in a sandwich ELISA.

  • Detecting antibody is the second, enzyme-linked antibody added after antigen capture, not the first immobilized reagent.

posts.post_title: In competitive ELISA for antibody detection,…
posts.post_content: In competitive ELISA for antibody detection, a positive test result (presence of antibody in test serum) is indicated by:

_aimcq_options.text: No change in color at all

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Decreased color production

In competitive ELISA for antibody detection, presence of antibody in test serum causes decreased color production.

The test serum antibody competes with pretitrated labeled antibody for antigen binding sites, reducing the amount of pretitrated antibody detected.

  • 'Increased color production' would suggest more pretitrated antibody bound, the opposite of a positive (antibody-present) result.

posts.post_title: Dot ELISA differs from standard plate ELISA…
posts.post_content: Dot ELISA differs from standard plate ELISA mainly by using which solid phase, allowing field use without sophisticated readers?

Dot ELISA uses a nitrocellulose membrane as the solid phase instead of a polystyrene plate, allowing visual reading without ELISA readers.

posts.post_title: The immunoperoxidase test (IPT) uses which c…
posts.post_content: The immunoperoxidase test (IPT) uses which chromogenic substrate to detect antigen in tissue sections?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: DAB (diaminobenzidine)

The immunoperoxidase test uses DAB, producing a brown deposit at the site of antigen, visible by light microscopy.

Unlike fluorescence-based FAT, IPT can be viewed with standard light microscopy on paraffin or resin-embedded sections without UV equipment.

  • FITC is a fluorescent label used in immunofluorescence assays, not IPT's chromogenic detection.

  • Horseradish peroxidase and alkaline phosphatase are commonly used IPT enzymes.

posts.post_title: Western blotting separates proteins using SD…
posts.post_content: Western blotting separates proteins using SDS-PAGE before transferring them to a membrane; it is named for its similarity to which other blotting technique that detects DNA fragments?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Southern blotting

Western blotting is named by analogy to Southern blotting, the technique that detects DNA fragments.

This naming convention followed Edwin Southern's original DNA blot method; Northern blotting (for RNA) and Western blotting (for protein) extended the wordplay.

  • Northern blotting detects mRNA, and it is Western blotting's counterpart, not the technique it was named after for DNA detection.

posts.post_title: The Ascoli precipitin ring test is classical…
posts.post_content: The Ascoli precipitin ring test is classically used for the diagnosis of which disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Anthrax

The precipitin ring test, also known as Ascoli's test, is classically used for anthrax diagnosis.

Correct Option Explanation

Antigen is carefully layered over antiserum without mixing; a precipitate forms at the interface if the reagents are homologous.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rabies diagnosis relies on direct fluorescent antibody testing of brain tissue, not the precipitin ring test.

Know More
  • Precipitation requires bivalent antibody and bivalent/polyvalent antigen.

posts.post_title: In the Ouchterlony double diffusion test, fo…
posts.post_content: In the Ouchterlony double diffusion test, formation of a 'spur' where precipitin lines meet indicates:

_aimcq_options.text: Partial identity between antigens sharing one epitope but not another
Absence of antibody in the well

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

  • Complete identity is shown by the two precipitin lines joining smoothly into one continuous line, not a spur.

posts.post_title: The Mancini test (single diffusion in two di…
posts.post_content: The Mancini test (single diffusion in two dimensions) is primarily used to:

_aimcq_options.text: Quantitate the amount of antigen present
Detect only qualitative presence of antibody

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Quantitate the amount of antigen present

The Mancini test quantitates antigen concentration by measuring the size/area of the precipitin ring formed around antigen-filled wells.

Correct Option Explanation

Antibody is uniformly incorporated in agar; larger antigen amounts diffuse further before reaching equivalence, producing proportionally larger rings.

  • 'Qualitative presence of antibody only' understates Mancini's specific quantitative antigen-measurement application.
  • 'Diagnose viral hemagglutination' is unrelated; hemagglutination inhibition tests serve that purpose instead.

  • Oudin test is single diffusion in one dimension.
  • Oakley-Fulthorpe test is double diffusion in one dimension.

posts.post_title: In rocket electrophoresis, the length of the…
posts.post_content: In rocket electrophoresis, the length of the rocket-shaped precipitate is directly proportional to:

_aimcq_options.text: The amount of antigen placed in the well
The molecular weight of the antibody
The pH of the running buffer

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The amount of antigen placed in the well

In rocket electrophoresis, the rocket-shaped precipitate length is proportional to the amount of antigen loaded into the well.

Correct Option Explanation

Antigen is electrophoretically driven into antiserum-containing agar rather than passively diffusing, deforming the Mancini-style ring into a rocket shape.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Molecular weight of antibody is not the variable measured; rocket length reflects antigen quantity, not antibody characteristics.
  • pH of running buffer affects migration conditions generally but is not the quantitative relationship being tested.
  • Temperature of incubation influences reaction speed but is not what rocket length is used to measure.
Know More
  • Rocket electrophoresis is a modification of the Mancini single diffusion principle.

  • Immunoelectrophoresis can resolve 25-40 distinct serum protein bands.
  • Counter immunoelectrophoresis exploits antibody's unusual cathodic migration.

posts.post_title: Counter immunoelectrophoresis (CIE) exploits…
posts.post_content: Counter immunoelectrophoresis (CIE) exploits which unusual property of gamma globulins to speed up the reaction compared to simple double diffusion?

_aimcq_options.text: Cathodic migration of gamma globulins under electric field
Their large molecular weight preventing migration

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cathodic migration of gamma globulins under electric field

CIE exploits the unusual cathodic migration of gamma globulins, while most other serum proteins migrate to the anode.

Correct Option Explanation

Applying voltage drives antigen and antibody toward each other from opposite directions, speeding precipitation and increasing sensitivity versus static double diffusion.

  • 'Large molecular weight preventing migration' is incorrect; gamma globulins do migrate, just cathodically rather than anodically.
  • 'Fluorescence under UV light' is unrelated to CIE, which is a precipitation-based, not fluorescence-based, technique.
  • 'Resistance to proteolysis' is not the property being exploited in this electrophoretic acceleration technique.
Know More
  • CIE is also called counter current or crossover electrophoresis.
  • The technique follows the same underlying principle as double diffusion but is faster.
  • CIE allows rapid diagnosis of several diseases.
  • Two-way immunoelectrophoresis further resolves electrophoretically separated antigen mixtures.

posts.post_title: The 'prozone effect' in agglutination reacti…
posts.post_content: The 'prozone effect' in agglutination reactions is caused by:

Absence of electrolyte in the reaction
Use of IgG instead of IgM

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

The prozone effect occurs when excess antibody coats antigenic particles so thoroughly that cross-linking and visible agglutination are inhibited.

Non-agglutinating (incomplete) antibodies with restricted hinge flexibility can also contribute to this inhibition at high antibody concentrations.

  • 'Excess of antigen only' describes the post-zone effect, the opposite extreme of the prozone phenomenon.
  • 'Absence of electrolyte' would impair agglutination generally but is not the specific definition of prozone effect.

  • Post-zone effect occurs with antigen excess.

posts.post_title: Passive haemagglutination converts a precipi…
posts.post_content: Passive haemagglutination converts a precipitating antigen-antibody system into an agglutinating one by coating antigen onto:

  • Latex beads are the solid phase for latex agglutination, a related but distinct technique, not passive haemagglutination.

posts.post_title: Which viruses can be identified using viral…
posts.post_content: Which viruses can be identified using viral haemagglutination and haemagglutination inhibition (HI) tests?

Newcastle disease virus is a classic example of a haemagglutinating virus identified and titrated using HI tests.

posts.post_title: In the complement fixation test (CFT), a pos…
posts.post_content: In the complement fixation test (CFT), a positive result (antibody present in test serum) is indicated by:

_aimcq_options.text: Absence of hemolysis (cloudy RBC suspension or button)

posts.post_title: Neutralization tests measure antibody's abil…
posts.post_content: Neutralization tests measure antibody's ability to block the biological activity of an antigen; an example application is identifying:

posts.post_title: The Gell and Coombs classification of hypers…
posts.post_content: The Gell and Coombs classification of hypersensitivity reactions was developed in which year?

Correct Answer: 1963

Peter Gell and Robert Coombs developed the four-category classification of hypersensitivity reactions in 1963.

This scheme divides hypersensitivity into Type I (immediate/IgE), Type II (cytotoxic), Type III (immune complex) and Type IV (delayed/cell-mediated).

posts.post_title: Type I hypersensitivity reactions are primar…
posts.post_content: Type I hypersensitivity reactions are primarily mediated by which immunoglobulin bound to mast cells and basophils?

Correct Answer: IgE

Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by IgE bound to Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils.

Allergen cross-linking of surface IgE triggers degranulation, releasing histamine and other mediators causing the acute inflammatory response.

posts.post_title: In cattle, acute anaphylaxis is primarily ch…
posts.post_content: In cattle, acute anaphylaxis is primarily characterized by pulmonary hypertension due to constriction of which vessels?
