Correct Answer: Pulmonary veins

In cattle, acute anaphylaxis is due to pulmonary hypertension from constriction of the pulmonary veins, causing pulmonary oedema and severe dyspnoea.

The main chemical mediators involved are serotonin, kinins and leukotrienes, with histamine playing a comparatively smaller role than in other species.

  • Coronary arteries are not the primary vessels implicated in cattle anaphylaxis pathophysiology as described.
  • Renal arteries constriction is not the characteristic feature of bovine anaphylactic shock.
  • Hepatic portal vein involvement is not the mechanism described for cattle anaphylaxis.
Know More
  • Smooth muscle of bladder and intestine also contracts, causing urination and defecation.
  • Heparin released from mast cells prevents blood coagulation in affected cattle.
  • Species vary in the target organs/systems affected during anaphylaxis.
  • Serotonin is a more significant mediator than histamine in cattle.

posts.post_title: Jersey cattle developing anaphylactic reacti…
posts.post_content: Jersey cattle developing anaphylactic reaction, urticaria and death from their own delayed-milking-induced protein absorption illustrates allergy to which self-protein?

  • Beta lactoglobulin from other cattle is not the self-antigen described in this specific milk allergy example.

posts.post_title: Type II hypersensitivity reactions are gener…
posts.post_content: Type II hypersensitivity reactions are generally described as being mediated by which mechanism?

Immune complex deposition in vessel walls

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Antibody (IgG or IgM) mediated cytotoxic/cytolytic reaction

Antibodies bridge antigen and effector cells or complement via their Fc regions, causing cell lysis, opsonization or antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC).

  • 'IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation' describes Type I, not Type II, hypersensitivity.

  • Type II hypersensitivity underlies blood transfusion reactions.

posts.post_title: Which condition results when maternal colost…
posts.post_content: Which condition results when maternal colostral antibodies destroy the red blood cells of a newborn that inherited a paternal RBC antigen absent in the mother?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

  • Serum sickness is a systemic Type III reaction from circulating immune complexes, unrelated to colostral RBC antibody transfer.

Know More

  • 'Aspirin only' is not identified as causing this red cell modification mechanism in the text.

posts.post_title: Isohaemagglutination refers to agglutination…

posts.post_title: The Arthus reaction is a localized form of w…
posts.post_content: The Arthus reaction is a localized form of which hypersensitivity type?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Type III

The Arthus reaction is a local manifestation of Type III hypersensitivity, involving immune complex deposition and complement activation.

  • Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated immediate reaction, distinct from immune-complex-driven Arthus reaction.

posts.post_title: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis in cattle fed m…

posts.post_title: Serum sickness, a systemic Type III hypersen…

posts.post_title: Live attenuated vaccines are prepared by whi…
posts.post_content: Live attenuated vaccines are prepared by which general process?

  • 'Complete chemical inactivation' describes killed/inactivated vaccines, not live attenuated vaccines.

posts.post_content: Which is a key advantage of inactivated (killed) vaccines compared to live attenuated vaccines?

posts.post_title: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) on phagocytes pri…
posts.post_content: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) on phagocytes primarily function as:

posts.post_title: Interleukins are cytokines primarily respons…

posts.post_title: Which lymphoid cell population is described…

posts.post_title: Which cell type differentiates from B cells…

posts.post_title: Which of the following is classified as a T-…

posts.post_title: Which ancient practice, preceding Jenner, in…
posts.post_content: Which ancient practice, preceding Jenner, involved inhaling powder from smallpox skin lesions to induce protection?

posts.post_title: Robert Koch is credited with describing whic…
posts.post_content: Robert Koch is credited with describing which immunological phenomenon in 1891?

Robert Koch described delayed type of hypersensitivity in 1891, an important milestone in cell-mediated immunity understanding.

posts.post_title: Which factor, according to this material, de…
posts.post_content: Which factor, according to this material, describes a good antigen having complex structure readily taken up by macrophages?

Complexity of an antigen's structure contributes to good antigenicity, as large complex molecules are readily taken up and processed by macrophages.

posts.post_title: Which property must an antigen have regardin…

posts.post_title: Regarding foreignness as a factor of antigen…

posts.post_content: Which statement correctly describes MHC restriction in cytotoxic T cell recognition of virus-infected cells?

posts.post_title: Which lectin pathway component, structurally…

posts.post_title: Which serological technique uses biotin-labe…

posts.post_title: The enclosed vacuole formed when a phagocyte…
posts.post_content: The enclosed vacuole formed when a phagocyte engulfs a microbe is called a:

Correct Answer: Phagosome

When a phagocyte engulfs a bound microbe, the cytoplasm forms an enclosed vacuole called a phagosome.

The phagosome subsequently fuses with primary granules (lysosomes) to form a phagolysosome, where digestive enzymes destroy the ingested microbe.

posts.post_title: Which nitrogen intermediate is produced by m…
posts.post_content: Which nitrogen intermediate is produced by macrophages via inducible nitric oxide synthase (NOS) upon stimulation with LPS?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Nitric oxide

Macrophages stimulated by LPS or other microbial products produce nitric oxide via the enzyme inducible nitric oxide synthase (NOS).

Nitric oxide combines with hydrogen peroxide or superoxide to form highly reactive microbicidal radicals within the phagolysosome.

  • The oxygen-dependent pathway includes reactive oxygen intermediates (ROIs).

posts.post_title: Which adhesion process describes neutrophils…
posts.post_content: Which adhesion process describes neutrophils losing flow speed and rolling along endothelial cell surfaces before escaping into tissue?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rolling followed by diapedesis

Neutrophils bind loosely to adhesion molecules, roll along the endothelial surface, then finally escape into tissues by diapedesis.

This sequence is triggered by chemokines and cytokines from damaged tissue or activated resident macrophages, guiding neutrophils to the infection site.

  • 'Direct transcytosis' is not the term used to describe this stepwise adhesion-rolling-migration process for neutrophils.

  • Chemotactic molecules like complement C5a guide neutrophil movement.
  • Vasoreactive molecules like histamine and kinins mediate inflammation.

  • Endothelial adhesion molecules are triggered by bacterial LPS or cytokines.

posts.post_title: Which important secondary granule component…
posts.post_content: Which important secondary granule component in neutrophils functions as an iron-binding protein?

Lactoferrin, found in neutrophil secondary (specific) granules, functions as an iron-binding protein, helping restrict microbial iron availability.

posts.post_title: Which cell type, upon fusion of its granules…
posts.post_content: Which cell type, upon fusion of its granules containing perforin and granzymes with a target cell membrane, causes apoptosis similarly to cytotoxic T cells?

NK cells, like cytotoxic T cells, use granules containing perforin (forming membrane pores) and granzymes (entering to trigger apoptosis) to kill target cells.

posts.post_title: Which cell type is described as constituting…
posts.post_content: Which cell type is described as constituting about 5% of total blood leukocytes and matures into tissue macrophages after circulating for several days?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Monocytes

Monocytes constitute about 5% of total blood leukocytes and, after circulating for several days, migrate into tissues where they mature into macrophages.

posts.post_title: Which factor is described as influencing gen…
posts.post_content: Which factor is described as influencing genetic species-specificity of disease susceptibility, exemplified by FMD virus not infecting horses and dogs?

posts.post_title: Which physiologic factor explains why birds,…
posts.post_content: Which physiologic factor explains why birds, with a body temperature around 42°C, resist many pathogens that grow poorly at that temperature?

posts.post_title: Which primary immunodeficiency example, invo…

posts.post_title: The germ line theory of antibody diversity p…
posts.post_content: The germ line theory of antibody diversity proposes that structural genes for all variable regions are:

_aimcq_options.text: Directly carried by germ cells, arising through gene duplication and mutation
Absent until somatic mutation creates them
Located exclusively on the Y chromosome

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Directly carried by germ cells, arising through gene duplication and mutation

Germ line theory proposes that germ cells directly carry structural genes for all VL and VH chains, generated through gene duplication, mutation and selection over evolutionary time.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts with somatic mutation theory, where a limited number of inherited genes diversify further during an individual's own development.

  • 'Absent until somatic mutation creates them' describes the somatic mutation theory's premise, not germ line theory.

posts.post_title: Which immunoglobulin domain structure includ…
posts.post_content: Which immunoglobulin domain structure includes hypervariable regions also called complementarity determining regions (CDRs)?

Constant domain of light chain only

posts.post_title: Which serum electrophoretic fraction, as ide…
posts.post_content: Which serum electrophoretic fraction, as identified by Tiselius and Kabat, contains albumin, the most abundant serum protein?

Correct Answer: Albumin fraction

The albumin fraction, distinct from the alpha, beta and gamma globulin fractions, contains the most abundant serum protein, albumin.

Electrophoresis separates serum into these four major fractions, with immunoglobulins concentrated mainly in the gamma fraction, distinct from albumin.

posts.post_title: Which structural feature distinguishes secre…
posts.post_content: Which structural feature distinguishes secretory IgA (SIgA) as a dimer compared to monomeric serum IgA?

_aimcq_options.text: Two IgA monomers joined by a J chain plus a secretory component
An extra CH4 domain not found in serum IgA
A pentameric ring structure like IgM

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Two IgA monomers joined by a J chain plus a secretory component

Secretory IgA is a dimer formed by two 7S IgA monomers joined via a J chain, further wrapped with a secretory component (Sc).

This structure, roughly 11S and 360 KDa, is much larger than the monomeric 7S, 160 KDa serum IgA form found circulating in blood.

posts.post_title: Which immunoglobulin class, according to thi…
posts.post_content: Which immunoglobulin class, according to this material, has an unclear or not well-established biological function and lacks interchain disulphide bonds?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

IgD has no interchain disulphide bonds, is susceptible to proteolysis, and its function remains not well established according to this text.

posts.post_title: Which regulatory complement protein displace…
posts.post_content: Which regulatory complement protein displaces C2b from C4b and Bb from C3b, thereby limiting convertase activity?

posts.post_title: Which condition described in this material r…
posts.post_content: Which condition described in this material results when lens protein escapes into circulation after eye trauma, causing autoimmune tissue damage?

posts.post_title: Which term describes autoantibodies produced…
posts.post_content: Which term describes autoantibodies produced against activated complement components such as C2, C3 and C4?

posts.post_title: Which infectious agents are cited as causing…

posts.post_title: Which cattle tuberculin skin test compares r…
posts.post_content: Which cattle tuberculin skin test compares reactions to avian and bovine tuberculin injected at separate sites on the neck?

posts.post_title: In cattle, the single intradermal test (SID)…
posts.post_content: In cattle, the single intradermal test (SID) for tuberculosis is typically read how many hours after tuberculin injection?

posts.post_title: The Johnin reaction, used to identify herds…

posts.post_title: In horses, tuberculin skin testing requires…

posts.post_title: Which skin test antigen is specifically used…

This reflects underlying differences in glycosylation and molecular charge among immunoglobulin classes, subtly influencing their electrophoretic behavior.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alpha-1 globulin fraction is not the mobility class associated with IgA or IgE in this comparative table.
  • Albumin is a non-immunoglobulin serum protein, unrelated to antibody electrophoretic classification.
  • 'Pure gamma only' describes IgG and IgD mobility, not the beta-gamma pattern specific to IgA and IgE.
Know More
  • IgM shows beta electrophoretic mobility, distinct from IgG's gamma mobility.
  • IgD, like IgG, shows gamma electrophoretic mobility.
  • Electrophoretic mobility differences historically helped identify and separate immunoglobulin classes.
  • IgG's low mobility places it firmly in the gamma globulin fraction.

posts.post_title: Which immunoglobulin class carries the highe…
posts.post_content: Which immunoglobulin class carries the highest carbohydrate percentage among the major classes described in this material?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: IgM, IgE and IgD (each about 12%)

IgM, IgE and IgD each contain about 12% carbohydrate, the highest among the major immunoglobulin classes listed in this comparative table.

Correct Option Explanation

In contrast, IgG has the lowest carbohydrate content (about 3%), while IgA falls in between at approximately 7%.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • IgG (about 3%) actually has the lowest carbohydrate percentage among the classes, not the highest as this option implies.
  • 'IgA (about 7%) is highest' incorrectly ranks IgA above IgM/IgE/IgD, when the text actually lists IgA in the middle at 7%.
  • 'None contain carbohydrate' is factually incorrect; all immunoglobulin classes are glycoproteins with defined carbohydrate content.
Know More
  • Immunoglobulins are classified as glycoproteins generally.
  • Carbohydrate content can influence antibody half-life and function.
  • IgG's low carbohydrate content correlates with its long serum half-life.
  • Sedimentation coefficients also vary distinctly across immunoglobulin classes.

posts.post_title: Which historical achievement is credited to…
posts.post_content: Which historical achievement is credited to Karl Landsteiner in the year 1917?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Description of the hapten concept

Karl Landsteiner described the concept of the hapten in 1917, expanding understanding of antigen specificity using small defined chemical determinants.

Correct Option Explanation

This built on his earlier and later work, including the 1901 ABO blood group discovery and the 1940 identification of the Rh factor with Wiener.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Discovery of ABO blood groups by Landsteiner occurred in 1901, a different milestone from the 1917 hapten concept.
  • Discovery of the Rh factor came later, in 1940, jointly with Alexander Wiener, distinct from the 1917 hapten work.
  • Clonal selection theory was proposed by Burnet in 1957, unrelated to Landsteiner's hapten concept contribution.
Know More
  • Landsteiner's hapten work used aromatic amines like aniline derivatives.
  • Haptens require carrier protein conjugation to become immunogenic.
  • Landsteiner's work helped disprove Ehrlich's side chain theory.
  • The resulting hapten-carrier conjugate is called an azoprotein.

posts.post_title: Which lymphoid tissue is described as probab…
posts.post_content: Which lymphoid tissue is described as probably the largest secondary lymphoid tissue in the body?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bone marrow

Bone marrow is described as probably the largest secondary lymphoid tissue in the body, despite also serving primary lymphoid functions for B cell development.

Correct Option Explanation

During secondary immune responses, memory cells colonize the bone marrow, which becomes a major source of IgG production in adult rodents upon re-exposure to antigen.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Thymus is a primary lymphoid organ for T cell maturation, not classified here as the largest secondary lymphoid tissue.
  • Spleen is a major secondary lymphoid organ but not specifically described as the largest in this material.
  • Single mesenteric lymph node is far smaller in aggregate lymphoid tissue mass compared to total bone marrow volume.
Know More
  • Antigen given intravenously can be trapped in bone marrow.
  • Primary immune response antibodies are mainly produced in spleen and lymph node.
  • Bone marrow's dual primary/secondary role is somewhat unique among lymphoid organs.
  • Memory cells colonizing bone marrow support robust secondary antibody responses.

posts.post_title: Which type of antigen specificity applies wh…
posts.post_content: Which type of antigen specificity applies when an antigen is specific only to a single species, such as species-specific antigens?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Species-specific antigen

A species-specific antigen is one specific in relation to a particular host species only, distinguishing it from organ-specific or cross-species heterophile antigens.

Correct Option Explanation

This category contrasts with organ-specific antigens (specific to a particular organ within one species) and heterophile antigens (shared across species and even bacteria).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Organ-specific antigen is specific to a particular organ within a single species (e.g., kidney vs lung protein), not defined by species-exclusivity alone.
  • Heterophile antigen is shared across different species and even bacteria, the opposite of strict species-specificity.
  • Syngenic antigen is shared among genetically identical individuals (e.g., twins), a narrower category than general species-specificity.
Know More
  • Frossman antigens are a well-known heterophile antigen example.
  • Alloantigens differ between individuals of the same species.
  • Autoantigens arise from an individual's own tissues under certain conditions.
  • Superantigens bypass normal antigen processing to activate T cells broadly.

posts.post_title: Which vaccine type is specifically noted to…
posts.post_content: Which vaccine type is specifically noted to have shorter-lasting immunity (usually less than six months), among the killed vaccine categories described?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bacterins

Bacterins, containing killed whole bacteria, are specifically noted to provide immunity usually lasting less than six months, a notable disadvantage.

Correct Option Explanation

Despite this shorter duration, bacterins remain advantageous for their ease of preparation and complete absence of reversion-to-virulence risk.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Recombinant DNA vaccines are not specifically characterized by this short six-month immunity duration in the text.
  • Conjugate vaccines are not described with this specific short-duration immunity limitation here.
  • Anti-idiotypic vaccines are noted for complexity and cost issues, not specifically for this short immunity duration.
Know More
  • Autogenous vaccines are a type of bacterin prepared from farm-specific isolates.
  • Fowl cholera vaccine is a cited example of an autogenous bacterin.
  • Bacterins are easy to prepare with no reversion to virulence risk.
  • Formaldehyde and adjuvants like alum are commonly used in bacterin preparation.

posts.post_title: Which antigen presentation pathway is used f…
posts.post_content: Which antigen presentation pathway is used for non-protein antigens such as glycolipids, presented via CD1 family molecules?

_aimcq_options.text: Presentation of non-peptide antigen via CD1
MHC class I endogenous pathway only
MHC class II exogenous pathway only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Presentation of non-peptide antigen via CD1

Non-peptide antigens like glycolipids and lipids are presented by CD1 family non-classical class I-like molecules, a distinct pathway from classical MHC presentation.

Correct Option Explanation

This pathway allows T cells, including NK T cells and gamma/delta T cells, to recognize microbial lipid-based antigens that classical MHC pathways cannot present.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'MHC class I endogenous pathway only' handles peptide antigens via TAP transport, not the lipid/glycolipid antigens presented by CD1.
  • 'MHC class II exogenous pathway only' similarly handles peptide antigens from phagocytosed material, not non-peptide lipid antigens.
  • 'TAP1/TAP2 transport pathway exclusively' is specific to peptide loading onto MHC class I, not the separate CD1-mediated lipid antigen pathway.
Know More
  • Endogenous antigen processing relies on immunoproteasomes and TAP1/TAP2.
  • Exogenous antigen processing uses phagosome-endosome fusion with MHC class II.
  • NK T cells specifically recognize CD1-presented glycolipid antigens.
  • Gamma/delta T cells also use CD1-restricted glycolipid recognition.

posts.post_title: Which serological test is specifically named…
posts.post_content: Which serological test is specifically named as useful for identification of bacterial strains using specific antisera?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Agglutination test

The agglutination test is specifically used for identification of bacterial strains using specific antisera, based on visible clumping of bacteria bound by antibody.

Correct Option Explanation

This application, alongside antibody detection in patient sera, makes agglutination a versatile and widely used classical bacteriological identification tool.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Radial immunodiffusion (Mancini test) primarily quantifies soluble antigen concentration, not bacterial strain identification via clumping.
  • Western blotting identifies specific proteins within complex mixtures, a different application from bacterial strain serotyping.
  • Complement fixation test measures antibody via complement consumption, not the direct visible clumping used for strain identification.
Know More
  • Brucella, Salmonella, Escherichia and Proteus form smooth suspensions for agglutination.
  • Flagellar, capsular or cell wall antigens are targeted in bacterial agglutination.
  • Slide and tube formats are both used for agglutination testing.
  • This is distinct from agglutination's use in detecting antibody in patient serum.

posts.post_title: Which statement correctly reflects the relat…
posts.post_content: Which statement correctly reflects the relationship between immunogenicity and antigenicity as defined in this material?

_aimcq_options.text: All immunogenic molecules are antigenic, but not all antigenic molecules are immunogenic
All antigenic molecules are immunogenic, with no exceptions
Immunogenicity and antigenicity are entirely unrelated concepts
Antigenicity requires T cell help while immunogenicity does not

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All immunogenic molecules are antigenic, but not all antigenic molecules are immunogenic

This material states that all immunogenic molecules possess antigenicity, but the reverse is not true—some antigenic molecules (like haptens alone) are not immunogenic.

Correct Option Explanation

Haptens exemplify this: they can be recognized by antibody (antigenic) but cannot induce an immune response alone (not immunogenic) without a carrier protein.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'All antigenic molecules are immunogenic, with no exceptions' directly contradicts the hapten example, which is antigenic but not immunogenic alone.
  • 'Entirely unrelated concepts' misrepresents the clear hierarchical relationship described, where immunogenicity implies antigenicity.
  • 'Antigenicity requires T cell help' is not the distinguishing feature described; the key distinction is about inducing versus merely being recognized by a response.
Know More
  • Haptens are the classic example of antigenic-but-not-immunogenic molecules.
  • Coupling a hapten to a carrier protein can confer immunogenicity.
  • Immunogenicity depends on factors like size, complexity, shape and foreignness.
  • Genotype of the recipient (MHC) also influences overall immunogenicity.

posts.post_title: Which term describes antibodies present in o…
posts.post_content: Which term describes antibodies present in one individual that are antigenic to some other individuals of the same species, such as blood group antigens?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Alloantigens (isoantigens)

Alloantigens (isoantigens) are antigens present in one individual that are antigenic to some individuals of the same species, such as blood group and transplantation antigens.

Correct Option Explanation

The corresponding antibodies formed against alloantigens are called alloantibodies, important in transfusion medicine and transplant compatibility testing.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Autoantigens arise from an individual's own tissue, provoking self-reactive immunity, distinct from the same-species inter-individual variation of alloantigens.
  • Syngenic antigens are shared among genetically identical individuals (e.g., monozygotic twins), the opposite of alloantigen's inter-individual variability.
  • Heterophile antigens are shared across different species and even bacteria, a broader cross-species category distinct from same-species alloantigens.
Know More
  • Blood group antigens are a classic example of alloantigens.
  • Transplantation antigens (MHC) are another important alloantigen example.
  • Alloantibodies can cause transfusion reactions if mismatched.
  • Graft rejection is driven substantially by alloantigen recognition.

posts.post_title: Which of the following best summarizes the f…
posts.post_content: Which of the following best summarizes the function of adjuvants when combined with a vaccine antigen?

_aimcq_options.text: Enhancing immunogenicity by prolonging antigen persistence and stimulating immune cells
Directly killing the pathogen in the vaccine vial
Replacing the need for any antigen at all
Preventing any immune response to avoid side effects

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Enhancing immunogenicity by prolonging antigen persistence and stimulating immune cells

Adjuvants enhance immunogenicity by prolonging antigen persistence at the injection site, enhancing co-stimulatory signals, and stimulating lymphocyte proliferation.

Correct Option Explanation

They are especially valuable when an antigen has low immunogenicity or when only a small amount of antigen is available, boosting overall vaccine effectiveness.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Directly killing the pathogen in the vial' is not the function of an adjuvant; that describes an inactivating agent used during vaccine manufacture, not the adjuvant itself.
  • 'Replacing the need for any antigen' is incorrect; adjuvants work alongside antigen, not as a substitute for it.
  • 'Preventing any immune response' is the opposite of an adjuvant's purpose, which is to enhance, not suppress, immune response.
Know More
  • Examples of adjuvants include alum, Freund's adjuvant and saponin.
  • Adjuvants can induce granuloma formation as part of their mechanism.
  • ISCOM and nanoparticles represent newer adjuvant delivery systems.
  • Adjuvants can reduce required antigen dose, lowering vaccine cost.
